texto: The summer after my freshman year of college, I
drove home alone from Denver to Indianapolis.
It's about 16 hours, and I'd convinced my parents I could do it in one day if I left
early enough. My dad made me promise to text
him every time I stopped for gas. I thought
he was being dramatic. That was 19, and I'd
never had anything bad happen to me, which
I think is the only reason anybody is ever that confident.
I left at five in the morning. Everything went
fine through eastern Colorado and most
of Kansas. I listened to an entire audiobook.
I stopped for gas outside of Salina around
six in the evening, texted my dad a picture of
the pump like I'd promised, bought a coffee
and a bag of beef jerky, and got back on I-70.
By the time it got dark, I was somewhere in eastern
Kansas, and the traffic had thinned
out to almost nothing. Just me and the occasional semi.
That's when I noticed the headlights. They were
behind me. Not close. Maybe a few hundred
feet back. At first I didn't think about it,
but I was driving a little under the limit
because I was tired, and normally people would
pass me. These didn't. When I slowed down,
they slowed down. When I sped up to see what
happened, they sped up, and kept the exact
same distance, like they were attached to my car on a string.
I changed lanes. A few seconds later, so did they. I changed back. So did they.
I told myself it was a coincidence, that somebody
else was just tired and following my taillights,
which people do. But it kept going. Twenty minutes.
Forty minutes. An hour. Every time
I checked the mirror, they were in the same spot.
Two round headlights, a little dimmer
on the left side.
I called my dad. I tried to sound calm, but
I don't think I did. He told me not to get
right up front. I opened my map, and there was
a truck stop about twelve miles ahead.
He stayed on the phone with me the whole way.
Every few minutes he asked, are they still
there? And every time I said yes.
The truck stop was huge. Rows of semis in the
back. A restaurant. A convenience store.
Bright white lights over everything. I pulled into
a spot right in front of the store, close
enough that I could see the cashier through the window. I watched my mirror.
The car pulled in a few seconds later. It drove slowly past the front of the store,
past me, and all the way to the far end of the
lot, where the lights didn't reach very
well. It parked facing my direction. Then its headlights turned off.
Nobody got out.
I sat there for ten minutes with my dad on the
phone. The car didn't move. I couldn't
see what kind of car it was. Just a dark shape.
Maybe a sedan? I couldn't see anyone inside
it. My dad said to go inside and tell someone,
so I did. I almost ran into the store.
The cashier was a teenage kid who didn't really know
what to do with me. But there was a trucker
at the coffee station who'd heard me. An older
man in a Carhartt jacket with a white beard
and reading glasses pushed up on his head. He
asked me which car. I pointed it out through
the window. He looked at it for a long time.
Then he said, okay, where are you headed?
His name was Walt. He told me he was going east anyway, and he'd follow right behind
me to the next big town, about forty miles. He
said if that car tried anything, it would
have to deal with eighty thousand pounds of truck
first. He gave me his CB channel, but
I didn't have a CB, so we just traded phone
numbers. My dad talked to him on my phone
for a minute. I don't know what they said, but
after that, my dad sounded a lot calmer.
We pulled out together. My car, then Walt's
truck, then nothing. I watched the far end
of the lot as we passed, and the dark car was
still sitting there with its lights off.
About five miles down the highway, the headlights
came back. They came up fast this time, much
faster than before. I saw them grow in my mirror
past Walt's truck, and I felt my whole
body go cold. Then Walt moved. He swung his truck
into the left lane, right next to the
car, and stayed there, matching its speed. Every time I tried to get around him, he
drifted over and blocked it. He called me and said, very calmly, just keep driving,
sweetheart. Don't speed. I've got him. It went on for maybe two or three minutes.
Then the car braked hard, dropped back, and
took the next exit. Walt stayed behind me
for the next forty miles. He followed me into
the parking lot of a police station in the
next town, waited while I went in, and then he
flashed his lights twice and pulled back
onto the highway. I never saw him again. I wish I'd gotten his last name.
I told the officer at the desk everything. I
didn't have a plate number, and I didn't
really expect anything to come of it. He took
my information, gave me a coffee, and let
me sit in the lobby until I felt okay to drive the
last few hours home. My dad met me halfway.
Two days later, a detective from Kansas called
me. He said a patrol car had found a dark
gray sedan abandoned at that same truck stop
the next morning, parked at the far end of
the lot. The car had been reported stolen four
days earlier from a woman in Colorado.
The woman had also been reported missing. He asked me a lot of questions about what
I saw, and I didn't have many answers. Then he asked me if I'd bought gas in Salina
that evening. I said yes. I'd texted my dad
a picture of the pump, so I even knew the
exact time. He said they'd found a receipt on the passenger seat of that car. It was
from the same gas station in Salina, Pump 4,
the pump next to mine. It was printed one
minute after my receipt.
